questions.prompt: You wrote five acceptance checks. After the parallel build, all five pass on the merged branch. What have you proven?
options: That the five behaviours you thought to check hold — anything beyond them is unestablished
That the task graph was correct, since the checks map to nodes one-to-one
Nothing, until a human reads every diff and approves it
questions.explanation: Verification is bounded by the checks you wrote: a green suite proves five behaviours and is silent about the sixth you never thought to name. Option A is the tempting one — 'all green means done' — and it is the exact mistake the verify step exists to prevent, because the empty-query bug that started this lesson would have sat in an unchecked behaviour. C confuses the verifier with the graph: nodes being satisfiable says nothing about whether you decomposed the work correctly. D overcorrects: the checks do prove those five things, and refusing to trust any evidence is not rigour, it is paralysis.

questions.prompt: Three nodes: A adds a `searchMode` option to config, B implements the empty-query guard against config, C writes the empty-query test. You mark A→B and A→C, then run B and C at the same time in separate worktrees. Both pass on their own branches. The merged branch fails C. What is the diagnosis?
options: One of the two agents produced bad code — re-run them serially and find which
B and C shared a decision neither owned (the guard's interface), so they were not genuinely independent; the edge belongs between them, or one node must own that interface
The verifier is flaky — re-run the suite on the merged branch
They should have been given separate worktrees, which would have prevented it
questions.explanation: Both nodes were individually green because each was self-consistent; the failure lives in the seam between them, which only exists after the merge. That is a missing edge, not a bad agent — file isolation held, and what leaked was meaning. A is the tempting one because a failure looks like a culprit, but 'find the guilty agent' cannot explain a defect that appears only in the combination. C is possible in general and is the wrong first move here: the failure is reproducible and logical, not intermittent. D inverts the lesson — separate worktrees are exactly what they had, and worktrees isolate files, not decisions.

questions.prompt: You decide to verify by reading the three diffs and re-running each agent's own tests, reasoning that each node already passed. Which class of defect does that method miss?
options: None — if every part passes, the whole passes
Defects that only exist in the combination: two nodes that are individually green and inconsistent with each other once merged
Only performance regressions, which unit tests never catch
Only defects in the checks themselves
questions.explanation: 'Every part passed' feels like it must transfer to the whole, and it does not: two nodes can each satisfy their own checks while disagreeing about a shared interface, a config value, or an ordering. That disagreement has no existence on either branch, so no per-branch run can see it. A is the assumption this question is testing, and it is the most common way a parallel run ships broken. C narrows the gap to performance and misses integration entirely. D is a real category but not what per-branch verification systematically misses — you can verify each check on the merged branch just as easily.
